name_en: Da Yu Ling High Mountain Oolong
processing: Minimal oxidation (around 10–15%), ball-rolled and dried without roasting, the lightest high-mountain style; the altitude rather than the processing defines it.
harvest_season: Usually a single late-spring pick in June, sometimes a small winter crop in October; at this altitude the bushes barely grow for most of the year.
appearance_dry: Small, dense, tightly rolled balls in a deep bluish green, visibly heavier and more compact than lower high-mountain tea.
appearance_liquor: Very pale yellow-green, thick-looking and bright.
appearance_wet: Small, thick, almost rubbery leaves on short stems, uniformly deep green with scarcely any red at the edge.
taste_profile: Cold, dense sweetness with pine and alpine florals, a creamy weight and a cooling finish that goes on long after you have swallowed; almost no bitterness even when pushed.

brewing.notes: Boiling soft water, a full dose and a long first steep to open the tight balls. Use a gaiwan and nothing else on the table; the point is a subtlety that disappears next to anything stronger.

vintage_note: What genuinely exists is sold by harvest, usually the June pick of the current year and occasionally a small October crop, in sealed 75 g or 150 g packs at prices well above Li Shan, often with the highway kilometre marker (95K, 101K, 104K, 105K) on the label. Since most leased gardens were cleared from around 2015 onward, supply is tiny and any cheap or plentiful 'Da Yu Ling' is a style name at best. It is drunk fresh, within a year, never aged.
description:
Da Yu Ling is the pass at about 2,565 metres where the Central Cross-Island Highway crests between Taichung, Nantou and Hualien, and the oolong grown on the slopes just below it, at roughly 2,200 to 2,600 metres, is the highest-grown commercial tea in Taiwan and among the highest anywhere. Gardens were known by the kilometre marker on the highway, 95K, 101K, 104K, 105K, and those numbers became shorthand for the very top of the market.

It is Qing Xin oolong made in the lightest high-mountain style: minimal oxidation, ball-rolled, no roast. At this altitude the bushes crawl, producing small, thick leaves with a lot of sugar and very little bitterness; a good lot has a cold, dense sweetness, pine and alpine florals, a creamy weight and a cooling finish that continues long after you have swallowed. It brews with the same approach as Li Shan: full dose, water off the boil, a longer first steep, and it keeps giving for ten or more infusions.

Here is the catch. Most Da Yu Ling gardens stood on leased national forest land, and from around 2015 the authorities began cancelling those leases and clearing the bushes to restore the slopes. Genuine production today is a small fraction of what it was, from a handful of remaining gardens, while demand has not dropped, so a large share of what is sold as Da Yu Ling comes from lower Li Shan gardens or elsewhere.

What exists is sold by harvest, usually a single late-spring pick in June and sometimes a small winter crop in October, in sealed 75 g or 150 g packs at prices well above Li Shan. Treat any cheap or plentiful 'Da Yu Ling' as a style name. Ask which garden, which marker and which pick, and expect the seller to be able to answer.

If you are paying for the real thing, brew it in a gaiwan with soft water and nothing else on the table; the whole point is a subtlety that disappears next to anything stronger.
sources_note: The garden-clearing timeline (leases on national forest land cancelled from roughly 2015–2016) is from memory of Taiwanese news coverage; the pass altitude is approximate. Which gardens remain in production today should be checked.
